title: Insomnia: Why you can't sleep
summary: Josh and Chuck explore insomnia: its definition, the 20-minute sleep-onset norm, transient, acute and chronic categories, the older primary/secondary classification (psychophysiological, idiopathic, paradoxical), and common causes including age, pregnancy, mental health disorders and medications. They cover prevalence statistics, sleep diaries, sleep hygiene (bedroom use, screens, exercise, bedtime yoga, regular schedules), supplements like melatonin, valerian and CBD, prescription sleep aids and their risks, the record-setting sleeplessness history (Randy Gardner), cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia with sleep boot camp and stimulus control therapy, passive wakefulness, and the counting-sheep myth. The episode ends with a listener mail from Nova.

segments.title: Tour dates promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote upcoming live tour shows in Orlando, Nashville and Atlanta and direct listeners to the website for tickets.

segments.title: Opening banter and insomnia introduction
segments.summary: Hosts banter about sleepiness and falling back asleep, then introduce insomnia as a topic they hadn't covered before, with sources cited.

segments.title: Sleep needs by age and aging sleep
segments.summary: Recommended sleep hours by age are given, along with the point that people get less sleep as they age, and the hosts discuss their own early rising habits.

segments.title: Definition and sleep-onset norms
segments.summary: Insomnia is defined as difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or both. Around twenty minutes to fall asleep is the normal range, and sleep-onset insomnia and worry about sleep are discussed.

segments.title: Consequences and insomnia statistics
segments.summary: Lack of sleep is linked to health problems and accidents. Prevalence statistics are given for Americans with sleep disorders and insomnia, and worldwide data on people not getting enough sleep. A sleep doctor's view that sleep problems are a modern phenomenon is mentioned.

segments.title: Causes and risk groups
segments.summary: Insomnia has many causes, mostly physiological arousal at bedtime, with possible genetic and age links. Women and pregnant people are more affected, and insomnia often co-occurs with depression and anxiety.

segments.title: Transient, acute and chronic insomnia; primary subtypes
segments.summary: Insomnia is classified by duration: transient, acute, and chronic (three or more days a week for over three months), with daytime impairment required. The older primary subtypes (psychophysiological, idiopathic, paradoxical) are discussed and noted as largely dropped.

segments.title: Secondary insomnia and medication causes
segments.summary: Secondary insomnia arises from another disorder and is the majority of cases. Triggers include depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and medications such as SSRIs, beta blockers and alpha blockers.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Sleep loss by decade and other high-risk groups
segments.summary: Sleep quality reportedly declines by about twenty-seven minutes per night each decade from middle age. Low-income households, chronic pain, diabetes, sleep apnea and restless leg syndrome are named as risk factors.

segments.title: Diagnosis and sleep diaries
segments.summary: Diagnosis starts with a doctor visit, where a sleep diary may be recommended to track habits like drinking, eating, exercise, and bedtime.

segments.title: Sleep hygiene and bedroom habits
segments.summary: Sleep hygiene covers habits and environment: avoiding screens, stimulants and alcohol before bed, exercise timing, bedtime yoga, consistent sleep and wake times, and a bedroom used only for sleep. John Hodgman's advice on large beds and separate bedrooms is discussed, along with the hosts' personal sleep experiences.

segments.title: TV and screens at bedtime
segments.summary: Watching TV in bed and screen light before sleep are discussed, with advice to move TVs out of the bedroom and use warmer screen settings.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Relaxation, passive wakefulness and supplements
segments.summary: Relaxation techniques and passive wakefulness are discussed, with advice to leave the bedroom during the day. Melatonin use is covered, including its source, short-term versus chronic use, and risks to children. Aromatherapy, valerian and tripping a fan are also mentioned.

segments.title: CBD and celebrity tangents
segments.summary: CBD sleep gummies are discussed as a wild-west area needing study. The hosts digress into a tangent about Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey possibly being related, and other celebrity-related anecdotes.

segments.title: Prescription sleep drugs and risks
segments.summary: Prescription sleep aids such as Ambien, Lunesta and ramelteon are discussed. They are meant for short-term use due to dependence risk, and sedative hypnotics can cause risky sleep behaviors. A butter anecdote follows.

segments.title: Sleep deprivation records and Randy Gardner
segments.summary: The history of sleeplessness record attempts is covered, including Guinness stopping tracking in 1997, Robert MacDonald's eighteen-day record in 1986, and Randy Gardner's eleven-day experiment in 1963 supervised by William Dement, with reported lasting effects.

segments.title: Cognitive behavioral therapy, sleep boot camp and stimulus control
segments.summary: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is described as the gold standard, including sleep boot camp and stimulus control therapy. An Australian study found five weeks of combined treatment effective without drugs. Most insomnia is treatable, but many people never seek help.

segments.title: Counting sheep myth
segments.summary: Counting sheep is described as not effective and possibly keeping people up longer. Researchers suggest imagining a relaxing place instead.

segments.title: Listener mail from Nova
segments.summary: A listener named Nova, a recent mechanical engineering graduate, shares how the show helped through tough times and inspired their studies.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank Nova, invite listener email, and close with the iHeartRadio production credit.
